papers.title: Target What? The Foundations of Poverty Targeting
papers.abstract: Most government transfer programs aim to target the poor. Doing so implicitly assumes that the lowest-consumption households have the highest marginal social valuation, i.e., have the highest social welfare gain from an additional dollar. But this need not be the case. In 600 Indonesian villages, we ask over 5,500 villagers to rank other villagers on how well off they are and how much a modest cash transfer would help them, and compare these rankings to consumption and self-assessed welfare. Targeting consumption misses 77% of households with the highest marginal social valuation. Targeting self-assessed welfare misses 57%. Even targeting those the community ranks worst off in levels, not margins, misses 25%. Divergences between different notions of neediness are statistically predictable. In a randomized controlled trial, proxy means tests best target consumption, self-targeting ordeals capture self-assessed welfare levels, and community targeting comes closest to marginal social valuation. Targeting strategies inescapably embed normative stances.

papers.title: Doing Better at Doing Good: Lessons from a Bayesian Meta-Analysis After 20 Years of Poverty Graduation Programs
papers.abstract: Multifaceted poverty Graduation programs that aim to increase income generating activities for low-income households are being rapidly adopted and scaled by nonprofit organizations and governments. This paper conducts a Bayesian hierarchical meta-analysis of 49 studies (encompassing 81 treatment variations) on poverty Graduation programs, defined as containing at least three of five components: consumption support, savings facilitation, skills training, coaching, and a lumpsum transfer. The analysis finds large gains across economic and psychosocial outcomes: monthly consumption rises by 38 USD PPP (11 percent), income by 28 USD PPP (15 percent), alongside improvements in savings, assets, food security, mental health, and women’s empowerment. Beyond these average treatment effects, three results stand out. First, programs with large transfers (at least 400 USD PPP) have larger treatment effects but are not more cost-effective. Second, more expensive programs generate larger treatment effects, but the improvements are not commensurate with the cost increases; thus, lower cost programs tend to be more cost-effective. Third, programs implemented from 2016 onward perform considerably better than those implemented prior to 2016: benefit-cost ratios from 2016 onward are 5.39, compared to 2.89 through 2015. Neither changes in cost nor in high-level design (components) explain this upward trend. Considering other heavily studied interventions, the results show a similar upward trend for treatment effects on behavior change from financial education but not for unconditional cash transfers. The paper hypothesizes a mechanism of continuous sector-community learning and improved implementation quality.

papers.title: Peer Influence in College Applications
papers.abstract: This paper studies how exposure to peers affects college application behavior. We use neighbors who attend different high schools to mitigate concerns about common shocks. Using granular classroom-level data, we find that exposure to peers who have applied to a program increases application rates. Consistent with an information mechanism, there is no additional effect of peers who are admitted. In counterfactuals, the effect is large enough to close urban-rural gaps and gender gaps in applications to selective college programs. We make the (generally NP-hard) application portfolio choice problem tractable using a setting where admission probabilities are observable and conditionally independent.

papers.title: When Food Stamps Became Free: Impacts and Implications of Removing the Purchase Requirement
papers.abstract: We analyze the food stamp program both as a potential investment in children’s health capital and as a redistributive tool by studying the 1979 reform that made food stamps free. We leverage geographic variation in exposure to the reform, which raised the program’s food subsidy from 65% to 100%. This raised enrollment by 1.85 percentage points (standard error = 0.15), or about 25%, with new enrollees substantially poorer than existing participants. From an investment perspective, we do not find evidence of improvement in infant health, and 95% confidence intervals rule out gains in birth weight from enrolling in food stamps exceeding 2%. From a redistribution perspective, the enrollment response implies that the average recipient of free food stamps acts as if they value them at 59 cents per dollar, with nonparametric bounds of 42–77 cents. Despite this substantial dissipation in transfer value relative to a frictionless cash transfer, under standard redistributive preferences the free food stamp program increases social welfare because of its targeting to very low-income households. The move to free stamps from a partially subsidized program improved targeting on social value but worsened targeting on private value.

papers.title: Beyond Overdose Prevention: Naloxone Coprescription Laws and the Path to Treatment
papers.abstract: Over one-third of U.S. states have enacted naloxone coprescription laws, requiring physicians to prescribe or offer naloxone alongside high-risk opioids. Using Medicare Part D data, the Treatment Episode Data Set, and a difference-in-differences design, we study how these laws affect naloxone access, broader prescription behavior, and treatment engagement. Coprescription laws increased naloxone prescribing by 275%, with effects twice as large in states requiring prescriptions as in those requiring only offers. We find no evidence of increased opioid or benzodiazepine prescribing, countering moral hazard concerns that broader naloxone access might encourage riskier opioid use. Instead, we document significant increases in prescribing of medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD) and gains in opioid use disorder treatment admissions, primarily in deliberate treatment-seeking settings. These results suggest that coprescription laws may have broader benefits beyond overdose prevention.

papers.title: Sorting by Participation: A Field Experiment in a Stem-cell Registry
papers.abstract: Unavailability of stem-cell donors at the confirmatory typing (CT) stage, an operational milestone in the stem-cell donation process, reduces the effective supply of life-saving transplants for blood cancer patients worldwide. Although (potential) donors register voluntarily, requests may come much later, when circumstances and commitment have changed; keeping registered donors engaged and identifying who will follow through are therefore central managerial questions for registries. In a field experiment with a leading stem-cell registry, we randomize the framing of routine invitations to an engagement initiative. Relative to a business-as-usual letter, our experimental letters present the registry’s requests more saliently; two of them add identity framings inviting donors to join a “quickly available” or a “highly committed” donor team. The salience and identity framings significantly reduce initiative participation compared to the business-as-usual rate, yet intention-to-treat analyses show no detectable effect on average CT availability. Our central finding is that participation sorts donors by reliability: participants are unavailable in 12% of cases, versus 30% of non-participants. From a managerial perspective, opting in works as a reliability flag. Prioritizing participants in our experimental arms implies a relative increase of up to 7.5% more one-year survivors compared to not using this flag. Gains from flagging are likely to be larger for registries with lower availability.

papers.title: When More Prenatal Care Looks Like Less: Selection, Information and Maternal and Infant Health
papers.abstract: We use Taiwan's 2003 SARS epidemic as a natural experiment, instrumenting prenatal care with gestational exposure to SARS-induced fear that reduced visits by over 20 percent. Adequate prenatal care reduces preventable maternal complications by 3.4 percentage points (26 percent), with no effect on infant outcomes. OLS estimates are perversely signed for maternal complications but overstate benefits for infant outcomes, consistent with competing patient- and provider-driven selection. Mechanism evidence points to prenatal care as a longitudinal information system: repeated contact facilitates detection of evolving risks and generates clinical information that informs delivery decisions, including delivery-mode routing and subsequent management at delivery.
